extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, students and scholars of drama/poetics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing classical tragedy: defining tragedy, its required parts (plot, character, diction, thought, spectacle, song), and precise rules for plotting (unity, magnitude, beginnings/middles/ends, peripeteia, recognition, avoidance of episodic structure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is an imitation of an action that is serious, complete, and of a certain magnitude; in language embellished with rhythm, harmony, and song; in the form of action, not of narrative; through pity and fear effecting the proper purgation of these emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasises imitation of action (not simple character-portraiture), the emotional ends (pity and fear leading to catharsis), and the use of embellished language (rhythm, harmony, song).

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal Limit (unity of time preference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy endeavours, as far as possible, to confine itself to a single revolution of the sun, or but slightly to exceed this limit; Epic action has no limits of time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer a compact temporal span for tragedy so the action reads as a single whole; epic may freely span long durations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six Constituent Parts of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Every Tragedy must have six parts which determine its quality—namely, Plot, Character, Diction, Thought, Spectacle, Song.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the essential elements to evaluate or compose a tragedy; two constitute the medium of imitation (Diction, Song), one the manner (Spectacle), and three the objects of imitation (Plot, Character, Thought).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot as the First Principle
rubrics_metrics.description: The Plot is the imitation of the action (arrangement of the incidents) and is the first principle and, as it were, the soul of a tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot determines the success or failure of a tragedy; other elements (character, diction, etc.) are subsidiary. Emphasise construction of incidents so they produce the intended emotional effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character as Secondary
rubrics_metrics.description: Character is that in virtue of which we ascribe certain qualities to the agents; it holds the second place after plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Character reveals moral purpose (what a person chooses or avoids) and is important, but should serve the action rather than replace it; a string of character-expressive speeches cannot substitute for a well-constructed plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (Dianoia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought is the faculty of saying what is possible and pertinent in given circumstances; found where something is proved or a general truth enunciated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thought supplies the reasoning and thematic statements within speeches; in tragedy it helps make actions credible and illuminating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction (Lexis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction is the expression of the meaning in words; its essence is the same in verse and prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refers to metrical arrangement and choice of language; precision and appropriateness of diction support the imitation but are subordinate to plot and thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Song as Chief Embellishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the remaining elements Song holds the chief place among the embellishments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Song (choral/lyric elements) is a principal ornament and occupies important parts of the play; incorporate where it serves the action and emotional effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectacle as Least Artistic
rubrics_metrics.description: The Spectacle has an emotional attraction of its own, but of all the parts it is the least artistic, and connected least with the art of poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spectacular effects depend more on stagecraft than on poetic art; do not rely on spectacle to substitute for proper plot construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of Wholeness: Beginning, Middle, End
rubrics_metrics.description: A whole is that which has a beginning, a middle, and an end. A beginning is that which does not itself follow anything by causal necessity; an end is that which itself naturally follows some other thing, but has nothing following it; a middle follows something and is followed by something.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A well-constructed plot must neither begin nor end at haphazard but conform to these causal principles so the sequence of events feels necessary and coherent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnitude and Unity of the Whole
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot must be of a certain magnitude—large enough for beauty but small enough to be embraced in one view or by memory; unity of action requires imitation of one whole action, not the many incidents of a life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid plots that are too brief to perceive unity or so long that the spectator cannot grasp the whole; unity is structural—if removing any part disjoints the whole, the plot is properly organic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Action (not unity of hero)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity of plot does not consist in the unity of the hero; it consists in centring the plot around one action such that displacing any part disturbs the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume one famous person's many episodes form a single plot; select and shape incidents that together form one causally connected action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry vs History: Aim at the Universal
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry relates what may happen (the universal), whereas history relates what has happened (the particular).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose tragedies to show how a type of person will act under probable/necessary conditions—names may be fictitious or real, but universality of action is the poetic aim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of Epeisodic Plots
rubrics_metrics.description: An epeisodic plot is one in which episodes or acts succeed one another without probable or necessary sequence; such plots are the worst.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Episodic structure weakens unity—bad poets produce them through fault; even good poets may create them to please players or stretch for competition, but they break natural continuity and reduce artistic quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprise + Causal Order: Best Mode to Produce Pity/Fear
rubrics_metrics.description: Events that come by surprise but follow as cause and effect produce the strongest tragic wonder; surprise plus a sense of design (not mere chance) heightens pity and fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct surprises (unexpected outcomes) so they are nonetheless the probable or necessary result of preceding actions—coincidences should feel designed, not accidental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple vs Complex Plots
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple actions are continuous without reversal of the situation and without recognition; Complex actions are those in which the change of fortune is accompanied by Reversal (peripeteia), Recognition (anagnorisis), or both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex plots (with reversal/recognition) are often more effective emotionally; choose form appropriate to the intended tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peripeteia (Reversal of the Situation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reversal is a change by which the action veers round to its opposite, subject to probability or necessity (e.g., the messenger who meant to relieve Oedipus instead reveals his identity and produces the opposite effect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reversal to shift fortunes decisively; ensure it arises from the plot's internal logic rather than accident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition (Anagnorisis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition is a change from ignorance to knowledge, producing love or hate between persons destined for good or bad fortune; the best form is coincident with a reversal (as in Oedipus).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The most powerful recognitions are those tied intrinsically to the plot's causal mechanics; recognition combined with reversal produces pity and fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal Causation of Reversal/Recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Reversal and Recognition should arise from the internal structure of the plot so that what follows is the necessary or probable result of what precedes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid external contrivances; the actions producing reversal/recognition must be motivated by earlier incidents and character choices.
